subject: Art & Design
title: Brand Voice and Tone
description: A micro-lesson that makes Brand Voice and Tone usable.

hook.text: Mailchimp's error messages are funny. A bank's error messages are formal. Same function. Completely different voice.

buildup.text: Brand voice is the consistent personality expressed through words. Tone adjusts by context (celebration vs. apology).

discovery.text: Voice is defined by traits: 'Bold but not aggressive. Warm but not sappy. Smart but not condescending.'

twist.text: Brand Voice and Tone has a twist: the obvious interpretation usually breaks down.

climax.text: Duolingo's owl is passive-aggressive in notifications.

punchline.text: Your brand voice isn't what you say. It's how people hear you.

quiz.question: What is the difference between brand voice and tone?
options: Voice is the consistent personality; tone adjusts based on context
Voice is verbal; tone is visual
There is no difference — they mean the same thing

details.summary: Brand voice is the consistent personality expressed through language — formal or casual, serious or playful, authoritative or friendly. Tone varies by context within the same voice.
details.whyItMatters: Inconsistent voice makes brands feel unreliable. When a company sounds corporate in emails but casual on social media, customers sense inauthenticity. A defined voice builds trust by making every communication feel like it comes from the same entity.
takeaways: Brand voice is personality; tone shifts by context
Mailchimp's guide became the industry standard for voice documentation
Inconsistent voice makes brands feel unreliable

faq.question: What is the difference between voice and tone?
faq.answer: Voice is the brand's consistent personality — always the same. Tone is how that personality adapts to context. A brand with a friendly, clear voice might use an upbeat tone in marketing but a compassionate tone when addressing a customer complaint. Voice stays constant; tone shifts.

faq.question: How do you document brand voice for a team?
faq.answer: List 3-5 personality traits with examples of what they mean in writing. Include 'this, not that' comparisons — 'confident, not arrogant.' Provide real writing samples for different contexts: social media, emails, error messages, and support responses. Mailchimp's public guide is an excellent model.
